rv.q: The attempt to draw parallels with the modern world through the climate crisis and fate of the whales is too obvious, and robs the play of its potentially fecund mystery.
The problem is that, like the ship itself, the play goes nowhere.
Dogstar deserves credit for its originality, in how it walks a tonal tightrope few could pull off.
Both witty and heart-rending, this Conrad-esque tale delivers laugh-out-loud humour and a startlingly surreal twist.
DOGSTAR is a quirky oddity with a few flaws but surprising charm.
However, despite top-notch acting from the three male leads, Dogstar is simultaneously too strange and not strange enough to warrant its 90-minute running time.
If you can forgive the static quality of the plotting, then this is an enjoyably ghostly excursion on a cold winter evening.
A strong cast did their best with what they were given, but what they were given was all over the place.
The show’s brilliance relies on the interactions between the remaining crewmembers and their interpretations of the reality of their situation.
An engaging, thought-provoking and powerful human drama.
It’s completely gripping and you spend an hour and a half completely absorbed by their world.
It’s a gripping, dark and entertaining tale and a perfect night out in the run up to Christmas.
Daisy Hall is an author of promise who is well served by cast and director of this fascinating glimpse into nineteenth century whaling life.

Lucy Morrison’s production is very watchable: it has an appropriately claustrophobic design by Hannah Schmidt, with Anna Short’s sound design of cracking ice and ominous rumbles providing a ghostly background.
The dialogue meanders unnervingly at times and touches on so many different styles and themes it loses dramatic drive.

Dogstar is an intriguing 90 minutes, simply staged by Lucy Morrison in Hampstead Theatre's intimate studio space, with Hannah Schmidt's timber beams and fluttering lanterns evocatively lit by Holly Ellis.
If that is the message, it could be delivered in a funnier package with a bit more dramatic tension.
The result is a play to which it is impossible to pay attention, because it seemingly has no idea where it’s heading and what point it wishes to make.
Dogstar is witty and imaginative, with some very funny exchanges that provide welcome relief from the increasingly claustrophobic and eerie atmosphere.
Amid the sharply written comedy and intimate conversations between the men, the mercurial establishment of what the men did, or did not, see, and how it resolves for them is absorbing.
Imaginative, thought provoking and a bit bizarre, “Dogstar” is a bracing breath of fresh air, but it could do with having a somewhat clearer idea of where it is heading.

cn.t: Hall's dark comedy about ice-trapped whalers offers sharp humor and strong atmosphere, but critics are divided on its static plotting and tonal shifts. Praised for wit and performances, yet faulted for dramatic stasis and narrative meandering.
